ques: the original Super Mario underground theme is literally only a 12 second loop. How did they get away with this?

ques: You said earlier that keys a minor third apart tend to be "ghost cousins" and while it could be argued that this is solely because that's the distance between a minor key such as D minor and its relative major , F, I was gonna ask do u think that movement between said keys can happen even if they are both major?

As I mentioned before you did this is "more than a dream" where the fact that the bit in D was major was hinted at by having a Gmaj7 in there, giving an F# in the melody. You ve said that this is a very natural movement and it does sound as such, so have you used this same harmonic technique in any other songs of yours?
answ: when i said that, i was specifically talking about when both keys are major (or both minor). if one is major and the other is the relative minor, i would consider those to be the same key. but indeed the reason that (for example) Fmaj and Dmaj slip so easily, is essentially the same reason that Dmin slips so well to Dmaj. (for the folks at home, you might know this as the "parallel major of the relative minor" of F). but the important thing is, this is not discovered by deliberately trying to slip a minor third. it's just simply by finding how you want the song to go, and go there. Zero times have i ever deliberately decided to do a minor 3rd slip on purpose. in fact, sometimes i am driven to avoid it and find some other amount to slip, just for something new

i'm not sure which thing you mean, but whether you are talking about slipping to minor-third-away sister keys, or landing in a new key on its 4maj7 with 3 note of new key in melody, both seem to occur quite frequently in my writing. again, in zero cases is this premeditated. the technique is to dive where i want to dive, and then let the analysts analyze later, which of course has no effect on the song, unless i notice certain maneuvers that are just happening way too often and then i try to avoid them for a while and find something new instead

ques: how do you go about writing a second verse when the melody is already pretty clearly defined by the first verse? i'm totally fine with writing the melody and lyrics at the same time, and i'm even decent at writing lyrics for a melody that has no lyrics attached yet at all, but writing lyrics for a pre-existing melody WHILE keeping it cohesive with already existing lyrics is shockingly difficult
answ: i have good news and bad news here. the bad news is, what you are trying to do, you cannot do. you are trying to 'write the song'. and you simply can't do that. this is extraordinarily bad news, unless you realize that the song actually wants to write itself. In the cases where you already have a first verse, and if the song wants to use that melody again, it actually comes extremely easy when the time is right. Actually, when it comes, it's likely that you may get a flood of 100 verses that all seem super good. but it never happens when you are in that frustrated mood of "i can't get this". it's a bizarre phenomenon, but just think of it this way: the song is going to come to you as soon as it feels it will be appreciated. and sometimes, when you're frustrated, you'd probably really appreciate some surprises, i bet

ques: there are different ways you add text to already shown subtitles: - the first one, you show the whole text at the start of a sentence. - the second one, you add words to the text and , if it's centered, it changes position on the screen - the third one, you add the whole text but it's masked and then you add words to that mask so, here's my question: how do you decide which method to choose?
answ: the second method you mentioned, in my opinion, always feels terrible and i never do it (unless by mistake). and the third one you mentioned i didn't understand your description. but here's my basic theory for it. first, some terminology... "word pops" is when the words appear one at a time. "cumulative word pops" means each new word appears, with the previous words staying there. "replace word pops" is when the new word appears and the old word disappears, with only 1 word ever on screen at a time. "entire phrase pop" is when multiple words appear at the same time. Generally, in my opinion, when doing cumulative word pops, it's very uncomfortable for the staying words to move when the new word hits. this is why your second option doesn't work for me. However, often, i might want the final result to have a centered feel to it. in that case, i actually use left justify and use spaces to get the final result how i want. then i do the cumulative word pops to work toward that, so the words don't jump. "Replacing word pops" usually means the words are fairly big, maybe even full screen. Replacing-wordpops tends to be uncomfortable if it's a normal (fast) paced sentence. replacing wordpops is usually best for like a 3 word sentence where all 3 words are strong and emphasized. Otherwise, when deciding whether to do cumulative wordpops vs displaying the whole thing all at once, this is what i've noticed: alltogether works better when the sentence is an already-known quantity. a typical sentence. in other words, when i expect the viewer to already know the sentence. in other words, it's a sentence with no surprises. such as: "how are you doing?" or "i'll see you tomorrow" or "i never noticed that". It's basically a sentence that functions as one word. it's a package deal that everyone already knows. That's when it's usually best to make the whole sentence appear at the same time. But when the sentence is more unique, or has surprises in it, that's when you want cumulative word pops. Another method, for different situations, is "letter type" where it appears one letter at a time, steadily. This seems to be best when it seems to be some kind of pre-written, impersonal, formal message

ques: you said in an earlier question that apples and oranges are the same while I completely disagree. would you care to elaborate
answ: there is currently an "apples and oranges" reference in common english, which has persisted for quite some time, and is still very active today, by which people always seem to mention "apples and oranges" whenever they are talking about any 2 objects which are "impossible to compare." it's "like apples and oranges", they say. It seems absurd to me, because apples and oranges are actually ideal for comparison. They are both fruit and have many similarities, and their differences are therefore quite obvious. They are just about the perfect thing to compare. So sometimes i am driven so mad by this constant sort of zombie-like widespread mindless obsession with "apples and oranges" being so "hard to compare" that sometimes i just blurt out that they are the same. ques: in "got some money", what was the purpose of putting "memory" in the cuts between "aaaacv" and "frenca", "frenez" and "loveqa", and "lovesz" and "zzzzya"?
answ: What i would have preferred to do, is to be able to actually create that entire alphabetical phrase list. which i was able to generate quite easily, but the problem we run into, when the list goes into the graphics, .... the list is so long that it actually makes the computer lag, or probably even crash, depending on how you do it. There's literally millions of lines in that text pattern, if it were carried out properly from a to z across all 6 characters. So even though it's just text, it actually is an absurdly unnecessary strain on the memory of the scene, pretty much any way you slice it. And the truth is, in that scene, with the small amount of time it's shown, you'd never see all the lines. and also, another reason you don't wanna include the whole list is that the scroll direction would become incoherently out of phase. like those car wheels on tv that seem to move slow or backwards or whatever. So it turns out, even just to create the proper looking downward scroll, you need to reduce the number of elements drastically. like pretty much skip 99% of the parts during the fast scroll. But this still does create a continuity problem, because if anyone sees the (maybe 1) frame where you can see it jump from A to L or whatever, .... i feel there's gonna need to be an explanation there. So my explanation is 'memory' as a place holder for the perhaps millions of lines we've skipped

ques: My list of song ideas, which are mostly just a few seconds of song each, is getting shockingly large. Like, it's well over a hundred, and I've only been collecting them for a year. I've written a few to completion, but it's always terrifying because I really really don't want it screw any of the songs up, because I kinda love all of them.
I hope to start recording stuff soon, but that's a stupidly large rabbit hole that I've yet to really touch. So.... what should I do?

Should I stop everything and focus on writing more for the songs I have? Should I just focus on trying to record stuff? I'm not really sure exactly what direction to go in, and this whole thing is feeling like a crisis at this point
answ: that's understandable
there are many good options here

talk it out, and you should start to see which way you want to go. new idea generation is always cool, you CAN continue to spend some time on that, however, if the guilt is killing you then you can suspend new gen for a while if it makes you feel more comfortable. If zero-record is k√illing you, then you can suspend all writing for a while if it makes you feel comfortable. Now, assuming you will record, choosing which one and which order is nearly impossible, especially for someone who 'cares' as much as i assume you do. I'm sure that every one of them has immense desire mixed with immense fear. this is normal. On one end of the spectrum, you could try to just go through the list and choose which one you 'fear the least', but this might actually make you pick the most boring one. You could do a brute force random, which means leave it to the computer to make a choice (count them up and randomize). And this may be a good idea but it also might not give you the best results. i've discovered that a hybrid method tends to work best for me, and it goes like this: go through your entire list, and pick out any one that excites you. and add those to a pre-selection list. And by the way, amount of writing completion shouldn't matter here. all of them are available, including ones at .01% writing. if it excites you, add it to the pre-selection list. Then, as soon as you finish the pre-selection list, immediately count them up and let the computer decide from there. and that's the choice. then finish the writing on that one, knowing it is the next one to be produced. then once the writing is done, then go into production. this hybrid method (half my choice, half random selection) has worked well for me for a long time, but, to be fair, that was long after i already figured out how to record a song. The problem i had earlier with recording songs is that it was too overwhelming, and what i actually had to do was write insanely short songs on purpose, so i could learn the ropes on everything quicker. so you might have to do that, if you are feeling overwhelmed with longer items. or who knows, maybe you won't be overwhelmed. but if you talk it out for a while, i'm sure you can come up with a great system that suits your needs. there are probably a million different schemes you could do, and the method you come up with can be something you are really proud of

ques: Helpppp in a moment of inspiration I started writing a song that I'm really happy with, but then the inspiration passed and days later it's still where it started and I can't seem to figure out what to do with it now
answ: this is normal, except for those rare cases where you can improvise an entire song. Most of the time you will find yourself in this situation, the 'second' half of the process, where you will be tasked to 'work' on the song, and find ways to coax or conjure up those inspirations again. i have some tricks. One trick is to just look to the original moment for answers. continue to tell the story of where you were and how you were when that first part came up. and another standard procedure is to run through the entirety of what you have, in order, in real time. another standard procedure is to ask categorical yes or no questions about it. "can it end here"? .... "does it want more of the same patterns?".... "does it want something completely different?" .... also another thing that happens is if you think about it for a while and then stop thinking about it, you might get the answer when you stop thinking about it. thinking scares music away sometimes

ques: how to stop getting writers block at the bridge of every song i make
answ: not that there has to "be" a "bridge", but let's assume you are talking about that place around 1 or 2 minutes where the whole regular cycle of the song seems to have expressed itself sufficiently (perhaps twice already), and the question is "what now?". This is similar to the feeling that you have just invented a peanut (or something) and now you have to figure out why that's important, or what to do with it, or where to bring it. and truly this can be a big question. here are some questions you can ask, if you haven't already: can the whole thing just end right there? (you'll know if the answer is yes, or no). can it be sent back around again for a third time, in some different way? ques: I've been thinking about how much something's/someone's reputation affects people's perception... If the Real Book was never published, would a whole new set of songs have become "the standards"?

Or what if Shakespeare never published any work when he was alive, and nobody ever heard of him until someone in the 21st century just happened to digup some chest in some old crypt that had all of Shakespeare's writings... would 21st century critics still be like "OK, this guy is the greatest playwright and greatest English writer of all time... we must make high school and college students study his work"?
Or if Jimi Hendrix wasn't on every magazine/internet list as the "Greatest Guitarist of All Time", would as manyguitarists still think of him as being so great?
I remember my dad playing me Hendrix when I was a kid and saying something like "Hey, listen closely, this guy's the best."

And very often, the ones that were big hits long before the book, are damn great in the book also, even without the lyrics. what tends to make something a 'standard' is if it endures popularity for many many years. ques: What do you want your songs to convey to people?

Actually I cannot point out what makes a song tick with me. Like with the Beatles' 'Yesterday', I like it but I don't understand why. I mean objectively it's a song about longing for a happier past, which is ... kind of ... lowly(Don't take this the wrong way, I feel there is some magic in the song but I can't explain it)? Like the right thing to do may be to move on right? So isn't it kind of... giving a message that it is ok to hang onto the past? But there are also songs about moving on like 'Let it go' from Frozen, which is sung in a situation when the character absolutely should not be moving on! But I still like the song. It feels like these songs don't capture the whole truth and I am finding it difficult to explain exactly what is the difference between them and absolutely lowly songs that only talk about sex, money, etc... that make me like them. If I were to make a song, I would want to give people the truth, or rather the peace or fulfillment that they want, but I also find that whatever I put into that song will be inadequate in doing so... How do you set standards for your songs in such situations, knowing all you can throw out there is incomplete and imperfect?

I am asking with regards to your own songs. Obviously you have high standards, a particular way of making songs that don't talk about lowly things. Like for example your song "might quit", which is about leaving and doing your own unconventional thing in a way that makes more sense to you... I cannot explain exactly but I tried doing that for some time in my life and it didn't work out... I realized it was just a pipe dream. So ...I'm ranting a bit... I guess I'm asking what is that thing of unending beauty that you can rely on?
answ: if i could explain it, then i probably wouldn't need songs to help me explain it

if you ever figure out what is 'right' or 'good', then it would never cease. like, literally it would be just one note held down for the entire time. if that's the best note, then keep it on. if there were a 'best note', then why do we keep switching notes? so in that case, the only thing totally 'not-imperfect' would be total blankness without any disruption. but that's not what we like about music, it's not what we like about games, it's not what we like about 'taking a hike', it's not why we're alive. we are moving beings

the entire world, but, also, any individual piece of that world is sufficient guidance. but i guess if you find yourself worrying about not being 'good' 'enough' 'all the time', then i suppose it's worth remembering that every picture ever painted has some lines that go in the wrong direction. otherwise there wouldn't even be anything in the picture. ques: I often find new artists through looking through the Wikipedia pages for certain genres of music. For example, I found the band Television Personalities while looking at the page for "Anti-folk," and I ended up subsequently listening to their album "And Don't the Kids Just Love It," all based on the fact that the picture for Television Personalities at the top of the Wikipedia page was really cool. Basically, all this combined gave me the impression that this would be a cool band, based on their name, genre, pictures, etc. When I listened to the album, it was good, but it wasn't as good as I expected it to be, even though I couldn't possibly have had any expectations for their music. Would you say my expectations based on things that had nothing to do with the MUSIC of Television Personalities in turn made my experience of their album less enjoyable?
Can that be applied to every artist? Is it best to just listen to a band's album cuz "fuck it?" as opposed to because "they looked cool," or "they had a cool album cover?"
answ: no, it possibly made your experience better, because you were in a welcoming mood

music discovery certainly works best when you are in that welcoming mood. because, at first, what else do you have? it's just the picture, the image, the title, .... you gotta start somewhere. so, indeed, these superficial attractors are a natural starting point. In fact, on some level i believe music actually needs something to latch onto, otherwise it doesn't even work so well. We've all had the experience of enjoying music in a video game. or maybe you'd go to a thrift store and see an obscure reggae record from 1973 that just looks magical. so you take it home and listen to it. Maybe it's good, maybe it's not, but being enchanted by how-and-where you found it, and the cover image, title, etc, certainly puts you in a welcoming mood, which will help you embrace all that may be good about it

ques: What do I do if I wrote a super awesome song outside of my vocal range? I can sing the problematic part an octave down, but it just doesn't feel right. I can also move everything down until it fits in my vocal range, but the lowest parts feel way too low then. Do I just hope and pray that I can eventually sing it as it is?
answ: among the things i would recommend, i do not prefer the 'octave-down' solution. However, i have 5 other semi-strategies (at least one of which you've mentioned) which all have their pros and cons. You can search for a compromise for the song's key, which sounds like it will be a tight squeeze because it sounds like the range of your song is wide. but, indeed, do what you can to find a compromise key. the next thing is just to keep practicing and eventually you will be able to sing a wider range. another option in the modern day, is to use computer assistance to produce the vocals outside of your range. the problem with that is, the results might not feel as genuine as you'd be able to get with your true voice, and also, if you ever are trapped in a cave with only an acoustic guitar, you wouldn't be able to perform the song, and also, in general there's a chance that it may hinder your growth as a singer because it might decrease your motivation to learn to actually sing it. Another option is to find a way to get someone else to sing it. the challenge with that, however, is that they just might not know how to sing your song as genuinely as you could, and of course maybe you don't even know how to find someone and/or incentivize them to do the job. Another option, of course, is to do a bit of re-writing to find a way that the song could comfortably land in a different key for that part. this may require some out-of-the-box thinking, but it can be done

ques: What do you think of Harmonic Minor Keys?

answ: it's really just a result of what happens when you are in the key of C minor and you use a Gmaj (or G7) chord

no, but i can explain why they have a word for it. it's because someone was noticing that a 'minor scale', in C minor, for example, seems to naturally want to contain these notes: C, D, Eb, F, G, Ab, Bb, C. But what happens, often enough, is you go to your big strong 5 chord and it's G7 which has the note B natural in it. and the melody may hit that B natural too. so the person was looking for a way to explain this so they said 'what the heck, just call it a new scale and say the B is always in it.' ques: Cab you explain the Pythagorean theorem For me
answ: sure. imagine a square, 1 inch wide and 1 inch tall. area is 1 (because 1x1=1).But how long is it diagonally? (wtf) longer than 1.... shorter than 2........ not 1 and a half........ what the heck is that number? got to be a super normal number, but it doesn't even seem to be in the same world as the 1. Anyway, try this: cut it along the diagonal to make 2 triangles. now take a second square and cut that one the same way. so now you have 4 triangle pieces. now rearrange those 4 triangles to make 1 big square. now you see, ... the height and length of the new big square is that ? mystery value from before. the area of the new big square is, of course 2. because you built this out of 2 original triangles which each had area 1. So what's the height/width of the 2 area square? in other words, what's the square root of 2? anyway, it's something point weirdsomething, but now you know a fun fact about the original 1x1 square, and what the heck that weird diagonal length was. indeed, it's the square root of 2. that should get you started

ques: okay i know that 4/4 means 4 quarter-notes in a bar, and that 7/8 means 7 eighth-notes in a bar, but what's a bar?
and what's a quarter note and a whole note?
does it relate to the tempo?
answ: a segment of time in the music, like those big sidewalk squares are a segmnt of the sidewalk

in most cases, a quarter note is 1 'beat' worth of time. a beat is typically the length of time that would recieve one foot tap, if you are foot tapping. in the normal time-signature (4/4) a quarter note is one beat. the 4/4 time signature is so normal that the quarter note (and thus all the notes) have been named in relation to a bar of 4/4. a quarter note is a quarter of the length of a bar in 4/4. and a whole note is the length of 4 quarter notes. in different time signatures, with different bar lengths, these names don't actually relate to the bar. the names are kept as if they are relating to a 4/4 bar, just because that's their name. at that point it's just a name

yes. the tempo is measured in 'beats per minute'. so indeed if you increase he tempo, it means the quarter notes will go faster, the whole bar will go faster. the whole song will go faster. tempo markings often show a little note to actually indicate what one 'beat' note is. ♩=100 means there are 100 quarter notes per minute. ♪=100 means there are 100 eighth notes per minute

ques: bill on 7.29.20 9:24 am you got a question saying " Have you ever got brilliant idea(s) while taking a shower but forgot as soon as you leave the bathroom? It sucks when that happens " and you said you developed some near military grade memory tricks for makign sure that doesent happen please bill what are the tricks
answ: here are some memory tricks. pretend you are explaining the idea to someone else, and start explaining it in as many technical ways as you can. Pretend you have to explain it to them so that they can reproduce the idea exactly, but, you are not allowed to actually demonstrate it. For example, if it's a sentence, say "the first word is ___, the second word is ____," etc... Count the words. remind yourself how many words there are. Say all the odd numbered words. Say all the even numbered words. Think of the first letter of each word, and put all those letters together. try to come up with an alternate sentence using the same starting letters. Try to access the idea in as many different ways as you can. If it is a musical idea, start thinking of the notation of it, imagine you are explaining the musical notation to someone else without singing it. List the notes in order. Count the notes. List the rhythmic values in order. If you don't know musical notation in this way, hopefully you have some other conceptual notation system you use to think about notes and time. What tempo is it? what song has a similar tempo? how many notes are in the first beat? how many notes are in the second beat? etc etc etc. Keep trying to access the idea on as many mental avenues as you can, and this will increase the likelyhood that you will be able to retrieve it. However, ...... if you've really just had the idea of a lifetime, and your life depends on it, then you can get out of the shower immediately and go write it down. it's a good feeling to know you have that level of professionalism

ques: hello, good evening, i hope you're doing well. music question: i'd like to make music, but for a myriad reasons never do, even when i have the time and will. one of the reasons is, of course, knowing that it'll never be as good as i want it to be. the only time i can feel at ease and just let things out is late at night when i'm improvising on whatever instrument, but that never results in a fully completed piece and any kernels that show promise never get planted and nourished, they're lost to the moment. which is fine, but ultimately i want to share the fruits of these moments with others. i've tried making them intentionally bad (usually when my friends ask me to make something for them), and that is definitely fun, but that method hasn't worked for my personal projects. wat do?

ques: why is the series of chords "4 5 1 6m" so absurdly powerful? (subbing the 4 for 2m also has a pretty darn similar effect) i've come up so many melodies that use those chords, and i love every one of them. i don't think i could make a bad melody with those chords if i tried. i'm aware that a million songs have used there exact series of chords, but somehow it never gets old. like, the bridge section in "do the thing" uses these chords and it's so, so fuckin awesome there. thoughts on why these chords always just.... work?
answ: i don't have any exact reason why that sequence might be good, but what i have done is extensively categorized and analyzed almost every common looping chord sequence. the ones that stood out to me as being the most reliably powerful, for me, were different from the one you selected. it probably varies from person to person. it's also worth noting that your sequence is a displaced 1,6-,4,5 or 1,6-,2-,5 which are traditionally known as extremely common. another thing worth noting is, categorically how does it make you feel when you start these things with 4 (or 2min). in my list of sequences, most of the ones i found to be most consistently the strongest also start with 4. For me, it probably tends to be "4, 1, 5, 5" or perhaps "4, 1, 5, 6-" that seem the most reliably strong. On the other hand, if we're talking about purely popularity, then it's hard to beat the infamous "6-, 4, 1, 5" which is almost certainly the winner in popularity, among chord loops, over the past few decades

ques: what's your compositional process?
answ: it's a combination of 3 main processes. start, select, and work. the key to these 3 things is treating them all like separate job positions. the "start" department dreams up brand new ideas, and it really doesn't matter how small the fragment is. it can come from almost anywhere. the "select" department chooses which one to produce next. the "work" department already assumes that one certain item has been selected, and then sees it through to completion. the piece wouldn't exist without the "start" department, but the marjority of the composition takes place in the "work" department. the key to the "work" department is to consider the actual real-time effect that the piece would have on you, and then let that trigger what comes next, as if by lightning. and being struck by lightning is of course completely impossible, or extremely easy, depending on whether or not it happens

ques: How to do the impossible task of convincing people to change a deeply entrenched habit that unnecessarily(changing said habit does not harm the person who changed) negatively affects others, when there are no visible, legal, physical, or social repercussions to such people in continuing to remain as they are? How can I do this successfully while still remaining doing my office job(as leaving job just to convince people may not pay at all,i.e., it may pay but it is extremely risky)? ques: is there a particular project of yours that taught you a lot while making it or is that just a standard thing for every project
answ: the one that really comes to mind is the parking lot video with all the cars ("Perfect"). this really solidified the phenomenon that if you do something 50 times, even if you are clueless the first 12 times, you start to find your way by about the 14th, and then you get super efficient by about the 25th. I watched this same exact phenomenon happen over and over and over again as i worked the assembly line in the modeling of 50 car models. from aligning the assembly line in the first place, to setting the initial shape and size, to wheels, to chassi, to roof to windows to plates to every little thing, done in the exact same order through all 50 models, and i watched the exact same cycle of cluelessness at first, finding the method somewhere between 10 and 20, and getting rock solid on it by the 30th. So reliable, makes me want to apply it to everything. And of course the other element of that car project, was the fact that i actually had to produce not 50 but 4000. And at such a high quantity, it requires me to invent/program a technique for doing it. If i only had to make 4 cars, i'd probably just make them all individually, and i won't really figure out what i'm doing. but if i have to make 4000, then i realize i can make 50 models to give enough variation, then i automatically learn a hell of a lot when tasked with propagating 50 to 4000, and also in making the 50. I vaguelly knew about all these phenomena before, but after doing that project it really made me realize the wide range of benefits that comes with unapologetically doing 4000 of something

ques: oh, ohhhh. okay so knowing scales is perhaps important to know chord nomenclature?
a major chord is the 1st, 3rd, and 5th note of the scale. a minor chord is the 1st, flattened 3rd, and 5th note. sus2 is 1, 2, 5. Csus4 is 1 4, 5?
okay but what's the difference between a minor scale and a major scale?
and the difference between playing in a minor and major key?
and a what is a major chord in a minor scale?
and can chords be shared by two scales?
fuck. how do i learn chords and harmony without learning scales?
i wouldn't mind learning scales but i want to play freely
answ: maybe
yep
C major scale would go like this: C D E F G A B C. and the C minor scale, at least the first part, goes like this: C D Eb F G. and the rest of it may depend on what the chords are at any given time

explaining this is like explaining the difference between a happy face and a sad face. it's not always possible to explain the difference, but you can just sense it. and of course some songs play tricks on you and kind of use both. other songs are very clear about it. jingle bells is major. "stayin alive" by the BeeGees is minor. generally, in a major key song, the "1" chord (sometimes called the "root" chord) would generally be major. and in a minor song, the "1" chord would generally be minor. now, how do you know what the root chord is? again, it's similar to knowing which side of someone's face is the top. how do you recognize this when a person is lying on their side? i have no idea, but you just know somehow

well, if you are in the key of C minor, it's fairly likely that you may hear some Eb major chords somewhere in the song, or Ab major or Bb major. Actually, it's fairly likely you may even hear the G major chord somewhere in a C minor song. that gets back to what i was saying about that part of the minor scale which tends to flex based on what chords are there
sure..... a C major chord would be likely to be found in the key of C, but also likely to be found in the key of G, or F, or A minor, or D minor, etc

no need to worry. just keep listening, keep playing, and let yourself be curious about whatever you find yourself curious about at any given time. it's all there for you, and also, it's magic, which sometimes makes it impossible to explain, but it's also the whole reason you're into it
in that case, my recommendation is to just never play scales in order. and also, as soon as you can, make friends with the 'chromatic' scale, which is just all the notes

ques: i've been working with the chromatic scale. my strategy is to let every note feel loved, and also to use the piano to lead the rhythm. it sounds very janky and awkward and dissonant, but there was a brief moment where i could hum each note before i played it at a not-very-fast place. i think i want to be able to do that faster: predict each note before i play it. but i wonder if my answer lies in intervals...

answ: probably more than half the time, the note you'd most want to sing might not actually be the root. if the chord is C major, the root of the chord is C. if the chord is C minor, the root of the chord is C
switching the notes around so the highest or lowest notes are different, but otherwise keep the notes the same. so switch the octave of one or more of the notes

you can invert it any way you want. put any of the notes in any octave. just be aware that if you have too many notes too low it will be harmonically useless and more like a horror sound effect, but that might be useful too in the right context

sure. chord names are never 100% accurate anyway. the only way to describe a chord exactly is to list the exact pitches that were played -- in fact, even that's not accurate enough to represent the exact sound. the only way to exactly represent a sound is with an actual sound wave

the next time someone sings the happy birthday song, try doing this: along with the final 2 melody notes in the song, you can sing above it. for example, if they are singing in the key of F, the last two notes are G F, so try singing Bb and A along with them. magic. ques: do you think feeling lost in life is related to decision fatigue?

could be
well in that case you weren't lost. being lost is when you actually have no idea where you are, in relation to where you've been, or in relation to where you're going

just start talking about it, and you'll start to sort it out. you said "what should the goal be" ... well, next maybe you'd think to yourself... "what is a goal actually?" "should i have a 'goal'"? "do i want to have a 'goal'"? depending on the answers to those, that will lead you to the next questions. basically you're just trying to get it down to one question at a time. if there's too many compounded questions at the exact same time, you actually can't perceive them, so it's just a foggy feeling. so you have to start sorting the mess of compound questions into something you can answer first. and the first several questions will usually just be about trying to figure out which questions you want to be asking

ques: Hi, Bill Fair warning this may be a long and somewhat abstract question, and I apologize if this kind of question has been asked and answered before. I've been a fan of yours for several years now and enjoy many of your songs. The lyrics especially have intrigued me and sometimes puzzled me throughout the years. I've noticed in the past when folks have asked you questions about the "deeper meaning" to the lyrics of your songs you coyly respond with answers that read something along the lines of "deeper than what?".

I'll admit, I once asked you a question like this several years ago on this pageand indeed received a similar answer. At the time I felt quite miffed, butthen I soon saw that many folks were asking this kind of question, and I believe I was asking the wrong question. You see, over theyears I kept thinking about this question I asked and your answer from time to time, and i think it started to make me ponder about the relationship that music artists can have with their songs, their fans; and the interpretation that their fans have of their music. I've seensome artists, when asked the question "what's the meaning of song [X]?", have a specific message in their mind they want song [X] to display, or perhaps a certain story they want the song to tell. In contrast, I have seen other artists not explain any specific "deeper meaning" to the songs that they make, and indeed these artists say that a song means whatever the listener feels they mean.

For example, your song "And The Day Goes On" (one of my favorites!): I like this song a lot, and to me, the "meaning" of the song is to persevere and press on when life gets stressful or tough. However, I understand that others may not interpret this song the same way that I do, and it really doesn't matter to me how others interpret the song - I like it for what it is for me. But this does get somewhat to the crux of my question, and it's a hard question for me to articulate because I've never tried to write songs before. I'm not looking forcontext about certain songs, but I am curious in general about the relationship artists may have with their published work. When you write songs, do they ever have a certain "meaning" to YOU?

Do you write songs hoping that your audience will interpret them in their own way and enjoy the song for what it is, regardless of what the song may (or may not) mean to you? Or is the process completely different? I'm curious about your thoughts on this idea.
Thank you and take care!
answ: that's because "deeper" is a comparison word (the "er" on the end). like "bigger, smaller", ... etc, if you use the word, you have to say the other thing we're comparing it to. sometimes people just say, like "is this lamp darker?" .... so i have to say "than what" because i need that second object to compare to. it's very hard to compare something to nothing. or at least i don't know how to do it
that's not how i react to the question -- almost every time, it's just the simple grammar conundrum, in the mechanics of the "er" suffix

yes, and the final song recording represents my best attempt at conveying that. if you find me using actual music/audio/song/graphic etc, then you can be sure that words alone weren't enough. in fact, they're barely enough now, to answer this question. i almost need music just to answer the question. so i'd certainly need music to express the things that i've used music to express. in other words, it would be impossible for me to express what i've had to use music to express, without music. indeed sometimes people come along and say something like, "can you express what you were trying to express in that music, except without using any music in your answer?" and the answer of course is no or i wouldn't have needed the music

the most profound meaning is certainly processed locally in the individual (within the mind of the person viewing/listening), so indeed it would be expected that everyone's peak meaningful experience might be slightly different. that's just the way it goes, in the 'feels' business

answ: not quite, i think the point i make is that that's probably not possible, and it may be unwise to try. i sometimes say it would be like 'painting with colors you can't see'

you can surely make things that other people like, by making things that you like, and then other people who have similar tastes to you will like it too. but if you are going against your tastes, then you'll actually have no idea what you're doing. again, like painting with colors you can't see. or baking with ingredients you can't taste. For example, you may notice that some other people like "slime" and you don't like such slime, if you say "well now i'll just make slime, and those people will like it", well, the thing is, those people obviously are seeing something in slime that you can't see. so if you try to make slime for those people, you'll have no idea how to make it because you don't know what they like and don't like about it. I just thought of a better example: let's say you are surrounded by people speaking a foreign language. you don't understand a word of that language: it sounds like nonsense to you. but you want to please the people who do speak it, so you try to write stories in that language. so you write the stories in nonsense because, to you, that's what that language sounds like. i think you see where i'm going with this

ques: I notice you seem to prefer traditional grip as a drummer, how did that come about?

ques: What should I do with my left hand when playing piano?
I usually just play chords with it but I never really see people doing the same so it must be wrong, any tips?
answ: what is your right hand doing, what is your voice doing, and what are the hands instruments and voices of the rest of the people in the band doing

there are many different roles a piano player may find themselves in. 1. you may be alone, singing a song and accompanying yourself with the piano. in that case, it's likely that your left hand will take the bass, and your right hand will take the chords, and your voice will take the melody. 2. you may be alone on the piano without singing. in this case you will probably be finding a way to generally cover bass, harmony, and melody, in various combinations of ways with whatever hands you can. 3. you may be in a small band with only bass and drums and piano. in that case, you will probably be responsible for melody and chords, in which case you will probably find your right hand doing a lot of melody (and some harmony) and your left hand lending some harmonic support where possible, and staying the heck out of the bass. 4. you may be in a band which includes a bass player and another melody player (or singer). in this case, again you'll want to stay the heck out of the bass, you won't need to be the main melody leader, and your main job will probably be just harmonic support. and in this situation, you'll probably want to be very careful about 2-handed playing, because most of what you need to do will probably be in a very one-handed range. if you insist on being very 2-handed here, you will probably be crowding the ensemble here 5. you may be in a band which includes a bass player, another melody player, AND also other harmonic players such as guitar. this case is similar to the above case, but even more delicate, and it's going to require some direct communication with the guitar player, to coordinate who does what. there's a lot of ways the 2 of you could ruin each other's lives, but as long as you are in communication then you can build exactly what you need, together all of the above situations are completely different roles for a piano player. this makes sense, because the piano actually contains the entire range of musical notes. so depending on who else is in the ensemble, you could be doing as much as everything or as little as nothing

i had more examples of things that instrumental music attaches to. but for brevity i only mentioned 2, but yours would have been next on the list. for example: you could be listening to instrumental music produced and delivered as just music, (and not produced as a soundtrack to anything), then, it's likely that you are aware of the identity/persona of the artist, such as name, what instrument they play, and maybe they even have a nice photo of themself on the cover, perhaps with the instrument. as you listen, you are aware of the person, almost like the way a movie star would star in a movie. so in that sense, the artist's persona is what anchors the music. Or, in another case entirely, maybe you are using the music as background music, and in that case it might be part of a broader collection/library of music, maybe even in some context where it doesn't matter who the artist is. In this case, being background music, the anchor element will be whatever you are actually doing in real life. Or, even more enchanting, would be if someone else picked the background music for their own location, in which you are a guest. so if you are in a store and there's music there-- this can enrich and enchant your experience in that location, and, in turn, your experience in that location will help anchor the music. you may even think back on that situation and feel great adoration for that song, meanwhile actually your experience of being in that store will very much help to anchor those feelings. If music actually were not connected or anchored to anything or anyplace in any way, then technically you wouldn't even be able to recall where or when you heard it, and possibly would have no memory of it at all

ques: lately ive been haunted by the notion that an instrumental song cant stand on its own (like it needs some other thing to go along with it). so i tried making songs with lyrics and i suck at it, and ive been sucking at it for quite a while now. but whenever i try to write a song w/o lyrics i think about that notion again and it ruins the whole thing. so i think i have to either use that thought to help me make lyric songs until im good at it, or i conbince myself its not true and just make more instrumentals. until i decide im in music limbo where i cant finish anything. do you have any thoughts on that original notion i mentioned at the start? or on the situation or whatev
answ: basically what you need here, is to dive head first into figuring out what really matters to you in the world, besides music. then incorporate that into music in a way that absolutely resonates with you genuinely. I too, spent most of my younger years wrapped up in only music (music music). so when it came to this point, what i did was, among other things, started freestyling text on a qwerty keyboard, from the abstract to the concrete, trying to really dig down to what means the most to me, and how i can genuinely find what i want to find, through language. after a couple of years of this, i felt more equipped with things to say and make music about, when i returned to songwriting. and i was pleasantly surprised that i was now doing it a lot differently from other songwriters, thanks to all that heck-the-out-tripping experience i'd had

ques: You know how in english (or at least american english, maybe there's different ones in other english speaking countries) there's those filler words like "uh" or "um" or "so" or "like", etc. What are some of the filler words you'd hear in dutch?
answ: you have uh/um. (those are pretty universal). you have "nou,", which is sometimes like the english "now," (when it doesn't mean "time"). sometimes "nou" is slightly more contradictory, like "well," in english. you have "dus" which is sort of like "so" but also like "thus" (which english doesn't use anymore). you have "soort van" which is literally "sort of", ... you have "eigenlijk" which is usually similar to "actually", you have "gewoon" which often is similar to "just", although it often appears in a different word order. you also have "even" (sounds like "effe"), which is a lot like "just" when it means "real quick". you have "zeg maar" (literally "say but") which means "so to speak", but maybe better aligns with english "i guess" added after something, for approximation. you have "een beetje" which is literallly "a bit", similar to british usage. you have "ik bedoel", literally "i mean", identical to english usage, and you have "denk ik" which means "i think" when added to the end of a phrase. you have "weet je?" literally "y'know". you have "natuurlijk" which is used like english "of course". and most of all you have "nou ja" or "naja", which often means something like "i mean yeah", or "well yeah,". And then, you have "lekker" which means tasty (or "tastily"), but it's somehow a filler word for almost all situations, whether it's something you enjoy actually or sarcastically

ques: why do you have two recurring answers, they're like running gags, on this page? they are: "i was going to say no but now that i think about it yes" and "i would prefer to make a new one to be my favorite"? like why do you keep saying "i was going to say no but now that i think about it yes" over and over instead of actually coming up with true proper and honest answers? why are those answers specifically the two running gags?
answ: first of all, i have more than 2 answers that recur from time to time. over the years with hundreds of thousands of questions, you're going to get that. "i would prefer to make a new one to be my favorite" is my honest answer to anything that asks me to choose a favorite amongst my own songs or videos. i resent the fact that you'd accuse me of being dishonest in that regard. the other one you mentioned, "i was going to say no but now that i think about it yes", is quite often an honest answer. again, i can't think of any reason you'd assume that's dishonest. This is usually the answer i give when i wouldn't have originally thought 'yes', but then after thinking about it for a moment, i realize, for the first time, that i do actually agree with the idea posed in the question. which in most cases would be something new to me at that moment. A small percentage of the use-cases for that answer are also because i just think that answer fits well with the question. sometimes it leaves room for the reader to think about it a little more, considering the implications of both a 'no' and a 'yes' answer, and the transition from one to the other. i find that answer to have a lot of different nuances depending on the question, so that's why i think i get so much mileage out of it

Or rather an Ebadd9/G/C :)

I guess the contrapositive here might also be interesting: If a chord looks exactly like a stack of thirds, is it possible for it to not be an extension? Like stacking thirds diatonically from C up to A,
is that always a C13,
or could it be a Bbmaj7/Cmaj?
What would have to be happening musically for it to be called a polychord?

that way might not be clear to anybody actually
i'd say that's a pretty typical "Cm13", as used in real life. to include the other notes might get too crowded anyway

Cm13, according to the notation conventions that i believe are still largely in play, in the professional music world, pretty much means that it includes precisely the notes you first mentioned (C, Bb, Eb, A) and this exact order you mentioned them is in fact seemingly the most useful and common, mostly

i almost wanna say you're not gonna find that in real life. the only place you might find it is in a textbook, and even so, that would be a textbook that cares more about what it looks like on paper than how it actually sounds in, like, ... music and songs and stuff

The C13 chord symbol, as it's actually used, is generally understood to have the following features: C in the bass, A somewhere in the harmony, Bb somewhere in the harmony, E somewhere in the harmony. then, less important, D is sometimes thrown in for support, and the G honestly usually just crowds things

ques: are there any songs where you wrote only lyrics first, instead of writing the lyrics with some instrument in tandem? if so, can you provide some examples of which songs (that you've posted) you did it with? and do you think writing lyrics before anything else affected the strong-ness of the song
answ: i've never done lyrics-first for more than one line (such as the title line). Lyrics first for an entire song can be a fun puzzle, and if you want to hear viable results of this, just listen to any Elton John song. but this method just doesn't work for me. However, what can be fun, is to dream up a title for a song. particularly something fairly long, where the title itself is fun to read. Then i'll take this line, musicalize it, and then continue writing the song from there. so only that one line was lyrics first. this is the only time where i'll use lyrics first, is only for a title line. Examples of this are "i like to wear soft clothing (cuz it makes me feel like i'm rough in comparison)", "the moon is made of cheese (but i can't taste it)", "ground plane", "the best thing about games is losing them", "i'm a huge gamer (most of the time)", and "the easter bunny told me that christmas isn't real (but santa claus is still jesus)"

The list will be quite long of course, but you will actually be pleased to find out that there are actually some things that don't fascinate you. those things won't make the list. ques: Hey, my question basically could be summarized as "how did you develop yourself as a musician?" (out of curiosity), and also, maybe, "how do you 'understand/(feel about)' music?", but unsure about that last one. Also, sorry if I ask too much and feel free to omit [not answer everything]. Relatively recently, I got more curious than I've ever been about music. And I found on the internet that you're self-taught and (from what I understand) that you don't really like music theory, and say that music can't really be described like that [sorry if I oversimplfy or misunderstand some stuff]. Which sounds kinda like the approach I would want to take to understand music better and/or maybe even write some of my own music later on. I think what sparkled my curiosity in music, was that some particular songs made me feel specific feelings, some songs being especially intense in that (a large amount of feeling ignited) [How did you get into music? (curiosity)].

So, that made me curious why those songs in particular and how do they make me feel such intense feelings [Do you have songs that made you experience similar things? Do you have the means (what sort of means? how did you get those means?) to explain that, or did you just accept the feelings without questioning them? (Other?)].

It seems to me that the two most important things in a song to me are "feeling" and "story". "Story" isn't necessarily lyrics; it could be fully instrumental song, it just may feel like the melody is still telling a story. And "feeling" is 'simply' the fact that melody evokes particular feelings. So, if I were to compose music, I feel like I would want to have these 2 [Do you have "similar" ideas about music, that you possibly apply to composing your own pieces of music?]
The problem is that I know like nothing about music, and when I'm behind the keyboard I basically can do only hit random keys,

and actually they sometimes provide some melodies(, etc) that sound somewhat adequate, and I actually made one into somewhat of a song. So, while this random hitting could provide some ideas, and maybe it is the way to discover music vocabulary, I am completely clueless as to how to transfer the feeling and the story with some sort of intent. And maybe my story/feeling idea isn't even the right approach to making music after all.
[How did you start to compose music, and how did that change over time?]

And finally, while I am at it (at asking bajilion questions): 1. How did you learn to sing while being self-taught? I would be curious to learn how to sing (at least a bit, for the sake of understanding music), but this one feels by far the scariest, as to not pick up bad habits, improper techniques, and not injure throat.

2. How did you develop your "ear"? In particular, how was the "the high class stuff" video made? The transcription of pitches of the speaking voice and the insane rhythms in it (weird rests ("offbeat"?), weird durations, triplets, quintuplets).
This text is so large so that I have to thank you just for reading it, and also thanks for answering on top of that.
answ: music is an irresistibly strong magical power. it's a no brainer for me to develop that to the best of my ability. the first time i got hooked on it was certainly too early in my life to recall. it was before i learned to speak

you can spend many lifetimes trying to explain exactly how this stuff works. i've certainly given it an earnest try from time to time. and as far as i know, no one really knows. although i'm sure someone will try to tell you they know

from all the years of trying to 'understand' 'why' this stuff works, or what's really going on, a few basic principles tend to keep emerging. one theme is "making patterns, and then breaking them", which of course can be applied recursively as the make-break becomes its own pattern which in turn can be broken. And another strong theme that comes up is the idea that you have to prove you're really there
right but as soon as the sound comes out you realize it's not random at all

i think with enough time and experience it's gonna work fine. like learning a language, it may take years, but inevitably you will get there if you just find a way to keep enjoying it and being curious

at a certain point you start to notice that you come up with ideas when you're not trying to, or when you're not supposed to. and then when you really try to, you clam up. gradually you start to learn how to strategically get that all sorted out, but it's taken me years upon years upon years upon years. maybe the first time i really wrote anything was like 6 or 7 years after i was first introduced to music, but then it was many many many many years later before i had anything with words in it, and then a few more heaps of years more before i did anything you've ever heard from me, surely

just doing it a lot, it usually gets better the more you do it. at some point i heard some hints about how to not hurt yourself, but most of the technical desctiptions of how to breathe and use this and that muscle and whatever, didn't make any sense to me. i've had far more success thinking of it in terms of acting. thinking of it as a form of communication

i'm not sure, but it occurs to me to ask you how you think you learned how to write and spell so well, in english. whatever mechanism that is, it's pretty much the same thing. and it also takes a lot of time probably

ques: Sometimes I think that it is unnessecary for me to know the distinction between turtles and tortoises. Why can't I just think that they are all turtles?

Like, only people who work with animals oughtto know that tortoises are different, since that's important for them. Butthen I realise that there's probably wayyy more comlicated and nuanced differences and facts about turles and tortoises and animals that they know and I don't, so I actually know a normal amount. And then I wonder why I'm soobsessed with limiting my own knowledge. Surely that can't be healthy, noropen-minded,
and I should cherish that I know turtles and tortoises are different, yes?
But then, what is the ignificance of the cognitive distinction, if it is likely that I will never need to pick one out of a crowd of the other?
Although, it's unlikely that a shark is heading straight for me, but it would help to know how to stop it from getting me. Should I relax on the whole knowledge thing,
or is there really no reason in seperating turtles and tortoises in my mind?
answ: you can. everything has to be approximated somewhere. do you realize how different some houses are from other houses, and yet the word house remains surprisingly useful

if you leave the turtle thing aside, this will only bring opportunities to learn other things that are more important to you. you're not obsessed with limiting your knowledge, but what you do have is a lot of analytical energy, to the point where you're on the verge of trying to open your mind in multiple ways at once, some of which may be contradictory to each other
there are equal joys to be had at every level of tortoise/turtle awareness spectrum
you may not need to, but what if you WANT to
you don't have to. i think your best bet at this point is to pursue your curiosities. the brain is maybe at its most powerful when it's curious. so you can't go wrong there
to put it in perspective, in some regions, the word for "soda" is "coke". so therefore Coke and Pepsi would both be considered different kinds of coke

ques: As I write more songs, I'm finding it's really easy for me to write choruses and bridges the repetitive or most important parts of the song that reveal the core way that I feel about something. These are usually the things I write first, the first things I come up with. As I then have to expand on those ideas, I find it's difficult to put together verses or pre-choruses. I feel like I'm out of things to say. I think part of the problem is that these are usually the parts of other peoeple's songs I find least interesting. Like, my favorite "musical moments" are often choruses or bridges, and I don't usually think about verses. Ofcourse there are great lyrical moments that I think about all the time, but those are few and far between I suppose. It's like, I just wrote the best part of this song, and now you want me to... write a less interesting part? I don't know how to expand on my ideas in that way. Does that make sense? What do I do?
answ: the first thing i'd absolutely recommend to any songwriter, forget everything you know about the names of the sections. "chorus", "verse", these terms play dirty and no one truly knows which is which, or if songs even need to have them, whatever. The important thing is, you've come up with the most important part, the best part. so you know you have that to offer. make the rest of the song about how good the main part is, and how excited you are to have people hear it. remember this 'additional contents' can be as short as you want, it can be after or before, in between, anywhere, and it does not have to be called a 'verse' or 'pre-whatever'. any amount of anything anywhere, in service of the main gift piece you are offering. in fact it's always good to first just ask yourself if maybe you don't even need anything else. and then just do whatever you need to deliver the goods. it's like you've got the birthday gift, all you need is the box. just put it in something and get it there, so it can be opened and enjoyed
